The system of household registration in the People's Republic of China, made national law in 1958. Every person is registered at a fixed place, and as either rural or urban, and that status decides where they may get schooling, health care, housing and pensions.

Household registers for tax and labour go back to ancient China. The communist version, set up in the 1950s, aimed to keep farmers on the land during the push for heavy industry, so that cities would not swell and grain could be taken cheaply from the countryside. In the years of the great famine it helped trap rural people where food was scarcest.

After the reforms of Deng Xiaoping from the late 1970s, hundreds of millions of rural people moved to work in the factories and building sites of the coast. Without urban hukou they often could not send children to city schools or claim benefits, so many left children with grandparents in their villages. Small cities have since eased the rules, but the largest still limit them, and the system still divides city from country.
